title: Rav and the porters' wages
hookLine: Jewish law protects both workers and employers
carry: wages before sundown; work with all your strength

cards: Porters are carrying wine for a man named Rabbah bar bar Chanan. Somewhere along the way they drop a barrel, and it breaks: wine all over the road. So he takes their cloaks, as payment for the loss.
They go to the teacher Rav and complain. Rav tells him: give them back their cloaks. He does.
Then the porters say: we're poor, we've worked all day, we're hungry, and we have nothing. And Rav tells him: go, pay them their wages.

teach.h: PAID BEFORE THE SUN GOES DOWN.
teach.b: First, the clock, in a verse this path met in Kedoshim. Leviticus says: "the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning."
Deuteronomy adds that a day worker is paid before the sun goes down, "for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it."
The Torah notices that someone is counting the hours until payday, and that the waiting itself is a weight. Second, beyond the letter.
When Rabbah bar bar Chanan asks Rav whether that's really the law, Rav answers with a verse from Proverbs: "That thou mayest walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous."
Commentators on this passage in tractate Bava Metzia read it as going beyond what strict law requires, because these were poor men who'd worked all day. Third, the worker's freedom.
The same tractate records a teaching that a worker may stop in the middle of the day.

The reason given is a verse: the children of Israel are God's servants, which the rabbis read to mean they are not meant to be servants of servants. Work is an agreement, not a chain. Fourth, the other side.
Jewish law also protects the one who hires.

Maimonides writes that a worker must work with all their strength, and points to Jacob, who told his wives he had served their father with all his power. Loafing on someone else's time is a kind of theft too.
So fair work runs both ways.

how: Jewish law codes devote whole sections to the duties of employers and workers, and some Jewish communities and organizations draw on these teachings in their own hiring and in public debates about labor.

o: a fixed wage set by the king for every trade
a rule that no one may work on the Sabbath
wages paid on time, and honest effort in return

p: give back the cloaks, pay the wages

s: the Torah lets an employer pay a day worker whenever it's convenient
Leviticus and Deuteronomy say a day worker is paid before the sun goes down.
in the porters' story, Rav tells the employer to pay them even after the barrel broke
he cites Proverbs: walk in the way of good men.
Jewish law only protects workers, not employers
Maimonides says a worker must work with all their strength, pointing to Jacob.

games.q: you're Rabbah bar bar Chanan. your porters broke a barrel of your wine. you've already given back their cloaks. they say they're hungry and have nothing. what does Rav tell you?
o: you're even now; they owe you nothing more.
make them work off the loss tomorrow.
games.why: Rav tells him to pay their wages too, citing Proverbs: walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous.

practice: Think of the people whose work touches your day: a cashier, a delivery driver, a cleaner, a colleague, someone you employ, or you yourself on the clock.
Pick one, and ask what fairness looks like there: paying promptly, tipping well, thanking someone by name, or one honest hour of your full strength. Hold that one act until it's clear.

wordCard.voice: Fair work: wages paid on time, beyond the letter when needed, and honest effort given in return. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: wages before sundown, and work with all your strength. Fair work runs both ways. See you in the morning.
